learningObjectives: Apply the full TDS1 workflow — Requirements, Attributes, Instances, Combinatorics, Classes, and Linking — to a business scenario from scratch.
Decide which combinatorial method fits a given scenario and justify the choice.
Apply independent capstone exercises without confusing planned data coverage with executed test evidence.

elements.description: This is an independent Quilyn worked example and set of practice prompts using documented Tosca design concepts. It is not a transcription or certification of the Academy capstone. Define business rules, modeled choices, expected outcomes, coverage method and traceability separately.

elements.text: The original Academy video and scenario files require access; their titles, contents and expected solutions have not been verified. Use the independent examples below alongside the linked primary documentation.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Worked example: a Loyalty Tier discount

elements.description: Independent assumptions: a checkout grants Guest 0%, Bronze 5%, Silver 10% and Gold 15% discounts on a subtotal of 100, before tax and shipping. An expired loyalty account is rejected. Assume Guest is the most frequent, least-dependent checkout path and a failure there has the greatest business impact. These are exercise assumptions, not facts about a real webshop.

Create a Requirement for loyalty-discount behavior and assess its risk using project evidence. The exercise does not determine a universal Frequency or Damage class from the feature name. Keep expected amounts and rejection behavior traceable to the specified business rules.

Use an optional layout with Administration (No), Precondition (Yes), Process (Yes) and Verification (Result). Model Loyalty Tier as the only varying business input; keep other inputs fixed for this exercise. Verification holds the expected amounts or rejection outcome.

Create Guest as StraightThrough under the stated frequency, dependency and impact assumptions; Bronze, Silver and Gold as Valid; Expired Account as Invalid. For subtotal 100, verify totals 100, 95, 90 and 85 respectively; for Expired Account verify the specified rejection and absence of a completed discounted order. Invalid data passes a test only when all relevant assertions hold.

With exactly one varying Attribute containing five choices and no constraints, Linear Expansion produces five datasets: one baseline and four alternatives. All Combinations also produces five in this single-Attribute case; it does not create an unnecessary larger suite here. Neither generation operation executes the tests.

A Class is useful if centralized sharing benefits other designs; a mandatory second-use threshold is not established here. Link the five design Instances to the Requirement as substitutes, replace them explicitly after linking physical tests, and inspect execution evidence and recalculated coverage separately.

bulletPoints: For this single varying Attribute, both Linear Expansion and All Combinations produce five design rows.
Verify each expected result explicitly; link and recalculate without equating planned coverage with passed execution.

elements.title: Choose and justify the test design
items: Discount rules: define the distinct outcomes and explicit expected amounts before choosing representative input data.
Product configuration: identify interacting choices and constraints; choose the method from required coverage rather than declaring a default.
Written billing specification: identify unclear rules, derive valid and invalid examples, and define observable expected results before automation exists.

bulletPoints: These are independent exercises, not certified descriptions of the inaccessible official capstone.

examPitfalls.title: Defaulting to All Combinations for every scenario
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Reaching for All Combinations whenever a scenario has more than one Attribute, without checking whether that's actually justified.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Choose the method from coverage goals, interactions, constraints and risk. No universal Linear Expansion default is established here; with one varying Attribute, All Combinations and Linear Expansion can have the same count.

examPitfalls.title: Skipping the Verification Attribute in a capstone TestSheet
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Building Precondition and Process Attributes but leaving Verification empty or undefined.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Define and bind the expected outcomes. A data Character, generated row or Requirement substitute is not itself an assertion or proof that a test passed.

examPitfalls.title: Using a fixed second-use rule for Classes
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Converting an Attribute structure into a Class the moment it's built, in a capstone scenario where it's only used once so far.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Choose shared maintenance deliberately and consider bidirectional reference edits. The accessed documentation supports reusable Classes but does not establish a mandatory two-use threshold.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Under the independent example assumptions (Guest is most frequent, least dependent and highest impact if it fails), why is Guest chosen as StraightThrough?

options.text: Because StraightThrough must always be the option with 0% value.
Its stated frequency, dependency and failure-impact assumptions match the StraightThrough criteria.
Because Gold cannot be marked as Valid.

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the StraightThrough criteria from Lesson 3: high-risk if it fails, easy to implement, fewest dependencies.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The choice follows the explicit exercise assumptions and documented StraightThrough characteristics. Guest is not inherently highest-risk or most frequent in every real application, and a zero discount is not the selection criterion.

optionExplanations.A: A zero percentage does not define StraightThrough; usage, dependencies and failure impact matter.
optionExplanations.B: The exercise explicitly supplies the characteristics needed to justify Guest as the baseline.
optionExplanations.C: Gold can be a valid business choice; that does not determine the baseline.
optionExplanations.D: The baseline is selected deliberately, not randomly.

practiceQuiz.scenario: With exactly one varying Loyalty Tier Attribute, one StraightThrough and four alternatives, and no constraints, how many design datasets does Linear Expansion produce?
practiceQuiz.hint: Count the baseline plus the four alternatives; these are datasets before template instantiation.
practiceQuiz.rationale: One baseline plus four alternatives gives five datasets. With only this one varying Attribute, All Combinations also has five possibilities; neither count is evidence of executed tests.

optionExplanations.B: One baseline plus four alternatives equals five datasets.
optionExplanations.C: There is no second varying Attribute whose choices multiply this set to sixteen.
optionExplanations.D: One covers only the baseline and omits all four alternate choices.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Five design Instances are linked to a Requirement as substitutes, but no physical tests have run. What does this establish?

options.text: The feature passed five executed tests.
The substitutes were automatically replaced merely by generating design data.
Planned design coverage, which still needs physical tests, assertions and execution evidence.
The application needs no further validation.

practiceQuiz.hint: A planning substitute and an execution result represent different evidence.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Substitutes represent linked design data, not executed or passed tests. Explicitly link physical tests, replace substitutes as appropriate, execute assertions and refresh outdated coverage values.

optionExplanations.A: No physical tests have run; planned links cannot establish a pass result.
optionExplanations.B: Generating design data alone does not replace substitutes with physical test links.
optionExplanations.C: This correctly limits the evidence to planned scope and identifies the remaining validation steps.
optionExplanations.D: The design still needs executable assertions and execution evidence.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An expired loyalty account is outside the valid business rules and should be rejected at checkout. Which Character describes this input, distinct from its test execution result?
practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the Character definitions from Lesson 3 — which one is used for cases that are expected to produce an error?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Invalid describes input expected to trigger an error. The test passes only if the specified rejection and all other relevant assertions are satisfied; the marker does not automatically invert the execution result.

optionExplanations.A: Valid denotes an accepted business input; the scenario explicitly requires rejection.
optionExplanations.B: Invalid describes the out-of-rule input for which rejection must be verified.
optionExplanations.C: StraightThrough is the frequent valid baseline, not this rejection case.
optionExplanations.D: Boundary is a Position property, not an alternative Character value.

quickRecap.value: Requirements → chosen Attribute structure → Instances → coverage method → links → physical tests and execution evidence.
Base it on how many Attributes truly vary together and the Requirement's risk — not a default habit.
Five choices yield five datasets under both unconstrained Linear Expansion and All Combinations.
Verify amounts and rejection explicitly; Invalid Character is not an automatic pass/fail inversion.
Derive choices and expected results from specifications; original Academy capstone contents are unverified.
